I am recording the work from the first inspection through the last rinse because the blue batch will be compared with the sample from March. The room was opened at six forty, and the wall thermometer read eighteen degrees. The night crew had left the exhaust fan running, and the floor was dry except beside the sink, where a narrow strip of cotton twill had been hung to drain. I moved it to the rack before bringing in the wool. The revised reading sheet should go to Leonie, not Emmett, because Leonie is keeping the comparison file and Emmett has the loom schedule.

Section one covers the incoming cloth. The wool came from roll W twenty seven and weighed twelve kilos six hundred grams after the paper wrapper was removed. The mill ticket listed a plain weave and a width of one hundred forty centimeters. There were two loose ends at the edge but no oil marks or visible stains. I cut the inspection strip from the marked end and wrote the roll number on its tag with the black laundry pencil. The cotton twill was a separate control cloth from bin C four, and it was not included in the wool weight. Both pieces were checked under the north window because the ceiling lamps make the dark yarn look warmer than it is in daylight.

The scour bath was prepared in the stainless tank with seventy liters of water at thirty eight degrees and a measured dose of neutral detergent. The wool stayed under the surface for twenty two minutes with slow movement by hand. I turned the folded center twice and kept the cloth away from the drain outlet. The first rinse ran clear after the third bucket, and the final rinse measured six point eight on the paper strip. There was no scent left from the detergent. I pressed water out with the wooden bar rather than twisting the fabric, then laid the wool flat on the mesh table for eleven minutes while the tank was emptied.

The dye recipe in the blue card calls for three hundred grams of indigo stock and forty five grams of the yellow modifier. For this run, I weighed three hundred grams of stock from bottle I twelve and used forty four point eight grams of modifier from jar Y six. The small difference is from the amount that stayed on the weighing paper, and I recorded the actual reading rather than rounding it. The water level was brought back to seventy liters before the stock was added. The assistant stirred for two full minutes with the broad paddle, then I checked that no clump remained at the bottom. The bath looked green under the room light and dark blue where it touched the side of the tank.

The wool entered at nine twelve and was worked slowly so the fold opened without pulling the selvage. I kept the timer beside the thermometer and turned the bundle at five minute intervals. The bath held between forty six and forty eight degrees for the first twenty minutes, then rose to forty nine when the heater cycled. The lid stayed partly open during that rise, and I reduced the setting by one mark. The cloth remained in the bath for thirty two minutes altogether. The exposed top edge showed a lighter band at removal, so I submerged that edge again for four minutes and noted the extra time on the log before lifting the whole piece.

The first rinse after dyeing was taken in a separate pail and came away blue green. The second rinse was less colored, and the third was nearly clear. I did not add soap at any stage after dyeing because the recipe card calls for water rinses only. The cloth was held over the tank until the drops slowed and then placed on the drying frame with the warp running parallel to the long side. The lower corner sagged about two centimeters, so I shifted the clips outward and checked that the edge was straight after the adjustment. The control strip went into the same rinse pails after the wool but was kept in its own labeled mesh sleeve.

At eleven thirty five, the wool was dry enough at the surface for a color reading, though the middle fold still felt cool. I used the handheld meter in three places and wrote down the values from the left edge, center, and right edge. The center was the darkest reading, and the right edge was slightly lighter. The difference was visible in daylight but not under the lamp. I did not describe the shade as a match because the March sample was not in the room today. The control strip measured more evenly across its width and showed a greener cast than the wool. I put both measurements in the margin so they can be compared when the earlier sample is brought back.

The drying frame was moved away from the radiator at noon after I noticed warm air reaching the bottom bar. The window remained closed because dust from the repair work in the hallway was still settling on the sill. The cloth stayed on the frame until two twenty and was then laid on clean brown paper with the tag facing up. I checked the selvage for dye transfer and found two small blue marks on the paper beneath the center fold. There was no mark beneath either end. I saved the marked sheet in the folder rather than discarding it and put a note beside the location of each stain so the next reading can be taken from an undisturbed part of the wool.

The final entry is for storage and handoff. The wool was rolled around a cardboard tube with the face side inward and tied at three points using the loose cotton tape from the worktable. The control strip was wrapped separately in clean tissue and placed in bin C four again. I wrote the batch date and roll number on both tags and left the dye card in the blue binder on the shelf. The temperature in the room at closing was nineteen degrees, and the fan was still running. The floor beside the sink had dried completely. I left the revised reading sheet on the desk in an envelope addressed to Leonie, not Emmett, and recorded that the March comparison sample remains outstanding."}]
